story_text.value:
I was finding that managing multiple agent threads with walls of text was getting tiring and inefficient for me and that I wanted a more visual way to interact with my agents, so I built Lynx.

Lynx lets you quickly build fully custom interfaces connected to your data sources (e.g. via MCP or API) and trigger agents running on your machine from them (e.g. with Claude Code or Codex).

I built it as an experiment but have found myself doing 80-90% of my work from inside Lynx. I have my own Conductor-like workspace for coding, a Mail client, a workspace for my writing, and various others for dashboards and explorations.

A few things are really cool about it:

- Adding buttons to a UI that trigger a Claude Code agent running on my machine (e.g. to review a PR, get started on a task from Linear, or look for typos in my text)

- Iterating on the interfaces is really easy, particularly because of a point tool that let's you select what you want changed and an agent will update it live

- Switching between workspaces takes a fraction of a second (much faster than e.g. switching between websites)

- It's all local :)

Harnesses have been moving towards native support for artifacts and MCP-UI which kind of go in this direction but I think the current models add to context fragmentation rather than actually help it, so I flipped the model on its head and built an AI workspace / harness where interactive interfaces are at the core.

Calling this an AI workspace for now but honestly unsure what the proper term should be. Is this a visual harness? A hub for personal software?

Keen to hear feedback about the conceptual model and what others have done that might be similar!

title.value: Show HN: Lynx – open-source fully-customizable AI workspace

story_text.value:
I run Claude Code on long tasks and walk away. When I come back, the one thing it needed from me is usually the last line of a long reply, three replies up, or it only ever said it in its thinking.

Handoffs gives those asks a fixed shape. Claude ends its reply with a short block that has a title, what it needs, why it can't do it itself, the steps, the command to run, and the choices. The mod turns that block into a card in a side pane, with checkboxes for the steps, Open and Copy buttons, and a button for each choice. Copy puts the command on your clipboard and never runs it. Open cards go back into the conversation after compaction, so Claude remembers what it's waiting on.

It makes no network calls. Cards stay on your machine and clear themselves after 14 days. MIT licensed. It needs Claude Code 2.1.299 or later and works best in /tui fullscreen.

Install:

  /plugin marketplace add ghosthat-studio/marketplace
  /plugin install handoffs@ghosthat-studio
I'd like feedback on the block format, and on what else should become a card.

title.value: Show HN: Handoffs, a Claude Code mod that puts each ask from Claude on a card

story_text.value:
Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that:

- I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath

- I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for

- Provided strong vm level isolation

- Hid credentials from agents

- Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace

- Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses

I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there.

Here's how it works:

Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested).

What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents.

Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console.

It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress.

Install:

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh
Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs

Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

title.value: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents

story_text.value:
Hello! I'm the solo founder/builder of FN2 AI and I built a free set of skills that you can use with an API key to dispatch research agents to search earnings calls, SEC filings, economic data, financial news, and more without having to set up all those sources yourself.

These agents can be invoked directly in a CC session, or scheduled at a certain time or to coincide with certain market events (Price Movements, Market Open, etc.), and it runs on self hosted infrastructure/k8s/custom stack that I maintain myself in two regions. I lean heavily into OSS models, and had a lot of fun building this.

I can talk at depth about things that have been working or not working if anyone is interested. Thanks!

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

Kakshil here, I am building an open-source tool which converts a folder of markdown files into an agent, which can be shared with a team with tool based access control.

The main goal with this was to have one "brain" or a folder, which I used to make my local Claude Code agents on, work for my team with checks, and also, run workflows on the server.

The same "brain" can be used for a chat agent or a workflow agent or an MCP server.

Try with:

  pip install hubzoid
  hubzoid init my-agent
  hubzoid run my-agent
Or use one of the ready to use agents, to get started quickly. Details in the readme.

It runs on Claude and OpenAI agents SDK, so the harness is borrowed.

It's apache 2.0 fully. Docs are here: https://hubzoid.com/docs. It runs with your existing claude or codex subscription, so no other api key needed to try it out.

Do try it out and share feedback. Happy to answer any questions.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Whisperstream, a free and open-source dictation app for Windows.

You've seen a dozen of these, so what makes it different from all the other dictation apps?

- Local cleanup: We're the only free and open source solution on Windows with a finetuned cleanup model. Stream-1 Mini is a Qwen 0.6B finetune for removing filler and applying spoken corrections. Superwhisper is the only Windows app that offers this, is paid, and in our benchmark we outperform their S1 mini with 36% less failures. Benchmark: https://whisperstream.io/stream-1-mini-vs-s1-mini

- Agent Speak: Hear or read response summaries from Claude Code or Codex, and speak back directly. Expand to see the full response without switching contexts. The TTS uses Kokoro for highly realistic voices.

- Smart Dictionary: Most local dictation apps don't offer dictionary support when using their fine-tuned cleanup model. We trained it into our finetune and use phonetic matching so we only include similar words for boosting.

It's GPL-3.0, completely free and now has a Mac version too.

Github: https://github.com/lanreal-io/whisperstream/

Demo: https://whisperstream.io/press/demos/launch-2.0-light.gif

title.value: Show HN: Whisperstream – Free, open-source local dictation for Windows

story_text.value:
Hi, here's a TUI we originally created for internal use. The goal is to be able to control multiple Claude Code sessions running in parallel while being able to review the changes and to understand the design choices the agents make.

The key design principles are:

- the programmer's attention is the bottleneck, so instead of cycling between sessions to find what's waiting for user input we use hooks to push work to the attention queue, i.e. let work come to you, not viceversa

- easy change, review and comment loop: [tuicr](https://tuicr.dev/}-inspired code reviews. Easy to add comments and send them to agents

- unobtrusive tooling: run on tmux sessions, connect to claude code via hooks, no complex dependencies

- quiz mode: answer design questions about the code to verify and reinforce your understanding of the changes

- keyboard-first navigation with vim keybindings

Comments, ideas and PRs all welcome!

title.value: Show HN: Aq – an attention queue TUI for Claude Code
